clue.text: Thief and fence in possession of 1000, policeman recalled

indicators.note: to be in possession of something is to hold it, so the fence holds the following letters inside it
recalled is read as called back, so the policeman's word is taken backwards

blocks.note: a picket is a pointed stake making up a fence
K, for kilo, stands for a thousand
slang for a police officer

explanation.surface: A thief and a receiver of stolen goods are caught holding a thousand pounds, and an officer is called back to the scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fence' looks like a second criminal beside the thief, but it is the picket that wraps around K and the reversed COP.
explanation.definitionFit: A pickpocket is a petty thief who steals from people's pockets and bags.

clue.text: Choose the best tool for breaking rocks

blocks.note: first meaning: to select the finest from a group
second meaning: a pointed implement on a handle used by miners

explanation.surface: Advice to select the finest implement for smashing stone.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for selecting the choicest and a noun for the miner's pointed digging implement.

clue.text: One of the Brontës, reportedly an impostor

indicators.note: reportedly means as people say it, so the answer is how the name is spoken rather than spelt

blocks.note: Charlotte Brontë, said casually as Charlotte 'un, that is 'Charlotte one'

explanation.surface: A rumour that one of the famous literary sisters was secretly a fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'Charlotte one' loosely, as 'Charlotte 'un', and it runs together into the word for a fraud.
explanation.definitionFit: A charlatan is a fraud who pretends to skills or knowledge they lack, so an impostor.

clue.text: Part of paper producing peculiar post

blocks.note: peculiar in the sense of belonging to one person alone
a post or pillar

explanation.surface: Some section of a newspaper is producing strange mail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peculiar' reads as strange, but here it is the older sense, special to an individual; 'post' is not mail but an upright pillar.
explanation.definitionFit: The personal column is the newspaper section carrying private notices and messages, so a part of a paper.

clue.text: Richest somehow acquiring medieval instruments

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters are got into shape in some unspecified way, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The wealthiest people have somehow got hold of antique musical instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: Citherns, or cithers, were plucked stringed instruments, close relatives of the guitar, popular in medieval and Renaissance times.

clue.text: One choosing to drop opener - might he make one cross?

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter, and it is dropped from the front

blocks.note: one who chooses, as a team selector does

explanation.surface: A selector decides to leave out the opening batsman; might that make the batsman angry?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry, but a voter marks a cross on a ballot paper. In cricket the opener is the batsman who starts the innings.
explanation.definitionFit: A voter puts a cross beside a candidate's name on the ballot, so the question describes someone casting a vote.

clue.text: Rosemary, perhaps, in feather bed

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows, across the gap between them

blocks.note: the end of feather joined to the start of bed

explanation.surface: A woman named Rosemary lies in a feather bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rosemary' poses as a woman's name; it is the plant, and 'perhaps' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosemary is an aromatic plant used in cooking, one example of the category.

clue.text: Soil shortage duke ignored

indicators.note: something ignored is left out, so the duke's letter is removed

blocks.note: a dearth is a scarcity
D is the abbreviation for duke

explanation.surface: A duke takes no notice of a shortage of soil on his estate.
explanation.definitionFit: Earth and soil are synonyms for the ground that plants grow in.

clue.text: Contestant after singer, a guitarist

indicators.note: after places the contestant's word behind the singer's word in the answer

blocks.note: a bass is a singer with the lowest male voice
a player takes part in a game or contest

explanation.surface: A competitor on a talent show goes on after a vocalist, and turns out to be a guitarist.
explanation.definitionFit: A bass player plays the bass guitar, so is one kind of guitarist in a band.

clue.text: Influence, by chance, quick early business meeting

blocks.note: power is influence over others
a lucky break is a chance
fast means quick

explanation.surface: Exerting influence, by luck, at a hurried meeting first thing in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By chance' reads as a phrase meaning accidentally, but 'by' only links the pieces and 'chance' is BREAK.
explanation.definitionFit: A power breakfast is a morning meal at which executives discuss business, so a business meeting held early.

clue.text: Seat I must sit in daily

indicators.note: sitting in something places it inside, so the single letter goes into the other word

blocks.note: taken as written
a daily, in British usage, is a cleaning woman who comes in each day, also called a char

explanation.surface: Someone told they must sit in the same seat every day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' seems to mean every day, but it is the British noun for a domestic cleaner, a charwoman.
explanation.definitionFit: A chair is a seat for one person, with a back.

clue.text: Incorrect ad bothers acting profession

indicators.note: something incorrect is wrongly ordered, so these letters must be put right in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An inaccurate advertisement annoys members of the theatrical world.
explanation.definitionFit: The boards are the stage, so to tread the boards is to act; the phrase stands for the theatre as a profession.

clue.text: In disarray, everywhere

blocks.note: first meaning: in a complete mess
second meaning: scattered in all places

explanation.surface: Things lying in a mess, scattered all over.
explanation.walkthrough: The British idiom has both senses: wildly disorganised, and spread across every place.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal British phrase means both chaotic and widely scattered in every direction.

clue.text: Fridge that is broken by clumsy mechanic

indicators.note: clumsy handling knocks things into disorder, so the letters of the tradesman are jumbled
something broken by another thing is split open around it, so the short abbreviation is parted to hold the rest

blocks.note: i.e., id est, means that is; 'that' is shared
taken as written

explanation.surface: A refrigerator which has been broken by a ham-fisted repairman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That is' gives IE, the abbreviation of id est, and it is split around the shuffled mechanic.
explanation.definitionFit: An ice machine is a refrigerating appliance that makes ice, loosely a fridge.

clue.text: Crystal getting rid of good sword

indicators.note: getting rid of something means removing it, here the letter for good

blocks.note: cut glass is fine crystal glassware
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Someone clears out their fine glassware and a decent blade.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutlass is a short curved sword of the kind used by sailors and pirates.

clue.text: Book about English County Council described by graduate

indicators.note: to describe a figure is to draw a line around it, so the graduate's letters encircle the others

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
a Bachelor of Arts degree holder
E is the abbreviation for English
CC is the abbreviation for County Council

explanation.surface: A volume about local government, written by a university graduate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Described' is used in its geometric sense: to describe a circle is to draw it, so the graduate's letters are drawn around the council's.
explanation.definitionFit: Rebecca is Daphne du Maurier's celebrated 1938 novel, so it is a book.

clue.text: Customers about right to send a message, briefly

blocks.note: c., circa, means about
a lien is a legal right to keep another's property until a debt is paid
telex, a verb for sending a message by teleprinter, cut short

explanation.surface: Shop customers are told they have a right to send a short message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' is not R here but a lien, a legal claim; 'briefly' drops the last letter of telex.
explanation.definitionFit: Clientele is the body of clients or regular customers of a business.

clue.text: Skirt around centre of Edinburgh in a taxi

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle, so only the middle letter of the city's name is kept

blocks.note: a miniskirt, a mini
ca., circa, means around
the fifth of the nine letters is the central one

explanation.surface: Someone in a miniskirt rides around central Edinburgh in a cab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like a container signal, but it is CA, circa. A minicab is a British private-hire car booked by phone, unlike a black cab hailed in the street.
explanation.definitionFit: A minicab is a car available for hire as a taxi.

clue.text: Obtains supply for a fortified place

indicators.note: supply is read as the adverb of supple, so the letters bend flexibly into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone gets provisions in for a castle under siege.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a noun for provisions, but it is the adverb from supple, flexibly.
explanation.definitionFit: A bastion is a projecting part of a fortification, and by extension a stronghold.

clue.text: Get hairdo in a place buzzing with activity?

blocks.note: first meaning: a tall domed hairstyle of the 1960s
second meaning: a busy place, and literally the home where bees buzz

explanation.surface: Getting your hair done in a bustling salon.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: buzzing is both busy and the sound of bees.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a towering bouffant hairstyle and a lively place, its literal sense being a bees' home.

clue.text: After duck, child tucked into cheese roll

indicators.note: after places the child's letters behind the duck's in the run that goes in
tucked into means put inside, so the run goes in the middle of the cheese

blocks.note: a soft French cheese
in cricket a duck is a score of nought, the shape of O
CH is the abbreviation for child

explanation.surface: Once the duck was finished, a youngster tucked into a cheese roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tucked into' suggests eating, but it means placed inside; 'roll' looks like part of 'cheese roll' but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A brioche is a soft sweet French bread, often baked as a roll or bun.

clue.text: Islander checks out writer

indicators.note: out means wrong or off the mark, so these letters are not yet in the right order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An island resident checks out a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Checks out' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'out' alone is the shuffle signal acting on both words.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Dickens was the Victorian novelist of Oliver Twist and Great Expectations, so a writer.

clue.text: Some of what's eaten on the ocean

indicators.note: some of points to a portion of the following words, letters lifted from inside them

blocks.note: running across what's and eaten

explanation.surface: Part of the food served aboard a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: To be at sea is to be out sailing on the ocean, away from land.

clue.text: Tide rising? Correct

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means read from the bottom up, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the tide is coming in, and is told yes.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit a text is to correct and revise it before publication.

clue.text: Night out? Not for me!

blocks.note: surface reading: an invitation to an evening of fun
setter's reading: someone who is never out for the night, in the sense of being knocked out asleep

explanation.surface: Someone turning down an invitation to an evening on the town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' sounds like going out, but it is out cold, asleep; the speaker is someone who can never sleep through the night.
explanation.definitionFit: An insomniac is a person who habitually cannot sleep, so is never out for the count at night.

clue.text: Correct an error in short advert recruiting soldiers

indicators.note: recruiting means taking people in, so the advert's letters take the soldiers inside

blocks.note: ad is the shortened form of advertisement
soldiers, as the men of a unit

explanation.surface: A mistake is put right in a brief army recruitment advertisement.
explanation.definitionFit: To amend is to change something in order to fix a mistake in it.

clue.text: Produced round cheese

indicators.note: turning something round faces it the other way, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: made means produced

explanation.surface: A dairy has made a wheel of cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round cheese' reads as one phrase, fitting the ball-shaped cheese, but 'round' is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Edam is a mild Dutch cheese, famous for its red wax coating.

clue.text: Wearing ceremonial garment causes speculation

blocks.note: dressed in, wearing
a vestment is a robe worn by clergy at services

explanation.surface: Putting on priestly robes sets tongues wagging.
explanation.definitionFit: An investment, putting money into shares or property in hope of a return, is a form of financial speculation.
